column5: Talking skulls were once said to have been found in the churchyard at Balsham. What became of them is not known.

Royalist Sir Hugh Piper is said to have set a Roundhead's skull in a niche at Tresmarrow House, and whenever it was buried the household suffered nightly knocks, voices and trampling until it was dug up again. After a spell in London being exhibited as Oliver Cromwell's skull, it returned to Launceston in 2001 and is now in the town museum.

A skull nicknamed Jimmy is kept in a cupboard at the General Burgoyne pub in Great Urswick, and touching it is considered bad luck. The cupboard sometimes opens by itself, and in 2016 a bar manager saw a faceless girl in a white nightgown pass through a closed door.
A skull at Brougham Hall caused trouble whenever it was taken away. To put an end to it, someone walled it up inside a room of the hall.

Wealthy magistrate Myles Phillipson framed farmers Kraster and Dorothy Cook for theft to get their land, and as they were sentenced to hang Dorothy cursed his family. Two grinning skulls then appeared on the Phillipsons' staircase and returned with terrible screams however often they were buried, burned or smashed.

A skull around a thousand years old was found in the basement of O'Lafferty's pub, formerly The George, in Derby. An entity blamed for switching off the beer barrels and causing general mischief may be linked to it.

Dickie, a skull on the windowsill at Tunstead Farm, was treated as a guardian, and taking it away even briefly was said to bring screaming and unrest. When the railway was planned across the farm, the works kept sinking into the marsh until the line was rerouted over what became "Dickie's Bridge".
Flagg Hall is said to be home to another of Derbyshire's screaming skulls. If the skull is ever removed, the house is said to echo with cries and moans.
A skull at Bettiscombe Manor is said to belong to an enslaved African man who died determined to be buried in his homeland. Any attempt to bury it anywhere else is said to make the skull scream aloud

A screaming skull kept in a recess on the stairs at Waddon was liable to be fractious and cause disturbances, so it was given to the Dorchester Museum. It was said to be the head of a Black servant, killed by mistake when his master took him for a burglar in the night.

Anne Griffith, youngest of the sisters said to have built Burton Agnes Hall, was attacked by robbers and asked as she died that her head be kept in the hall. Her sisters buried her whole, and the house was plagued by noises until her skull was brought inside, where it is thought to remain, walled up.
Freda's skull is kept behind the bar of Ye Olde White Harte in Hull. If it is moved, its former owner is said to haunt the building until it is put back.
A skull at a manor house in Lund was bricked up in the attic so that nobody could ever take it away. Little else is recorded about it, and it is unknown whether it is still there.

Two skulls are hidden in the walls of the ruined Warbleton Priory: one of a murdered prior and one of the man who killed him. Mayhem is said to follow any attempt to remove them, though one once stayed silent while a blue tit nested inside it.

An old brown skull behind the bar of the Pack Horse in Affetside is said to be that of George Whowell, the local headsman who executed James Stanley, 7th Earl of Derby. Rumour has it that the skull cannot be moved, or it will scream.

The skull at Wardley Hall is most likely that of Father Ambrose Barlow, a Catholic priest hanged, drawn and quartered in 1641, whose head was taken from Lancaster Castle and hidden in the hall's walls. When a servant threw it into the moat a terrible storm broke, and the owner had the moat drained to bring it back.
A nun's skull is kept at Pennis Farm near Fawkham Green, and removing it is said to bring a great curse on the whole valley. Her figure is reported floating down Pennis Lane at dusk in autumn.

Legend says the skull at Skull House in Appley Bridge belonged to a monk who hid in the chimney from the Roundheads and was smoked out and beheaded. Every attempt to get rid of it has ended badly: one man threw it in the River Douglas, found it back in its place, and later drowned in that same river.

A local girl's skull was displayed at Ripley's Odditorium in Blackpool, and several people reported a female ghost standing beside it. Its former owner believed it was cursed and died a week after giving it away.

Two skulls are stored at Turton Tower, and when they were kept elsewhere two ghostly men were said to appear and fight. The tower is also said to have poltergeist activity, a woman in mourning on the staircase and a phantom coach outside.
A skull in a cabinet at Browsholme Hall is thought to belong to a martyr of the 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace. Legend says dire things will happen if it ever leaves the house.

The dying Bran the Blessed ordered his followers to cut off his head and, after years of feasting with it, bury it on the White Hill in London facing France. So long as it lay undisturbed Britain would be safe from invasion, until King Arthur dug it up, choosing to hold the island by his own prowess.

Before his death in 1670, Theophilus Broome left instructions that his skull be kept at his farmhouse in Chilton Cantelo. Attempts to remove it are said to have unleashed poltergeist activity and havoc, so it has stayed at the farm.

The skull of William Corder, the Red Barn murderer, was kept at the prison in Bury St Edmunds and was believed to be evil. Strange sounds and figures were reported around it until it was removed and buried in a country graveyard.
Local legend tells of a pair of skulls that once sat in Long Melford churchyard. After dark, they were said to chatter to one another.

In 1968 workmen restoring Sowood House found a human skull in an iron box hidden in the brickwork, probably a 17th-century man's and perhaps placed there to guard against witches. An elderly local then wrote that it had been found once before and buried in Coley churchyard, and the house was haunted by cries of "Where's my head?" until it was brought back.
A woman's skull kept at the house at Pinkney Park is believed to belong to a young girl who was killed by her own sister. Her ghost is said to roam carrying her head under her arm.

The church of St Ursula in Cologne once had small boxes of skulls crowding its walls above the arches and below the clerestory windows. In later years they were hidden behind curtains, but the sacristy still looked like a charnel house.
Oliver Plunkett's severed head is often compared with the screaming skull of Father Ambrose Barlow, but it never screamed. Instead, it is said to have communicated with the living through miracles.

A maid at Ffagnallt Hall threw a skull she had been told not to touch into the horse pond, and that night the household found her in the pond clutching it and crying that the Dead Man's curse was upon her. The skull is said to be that of Dafydd ap Owain Gwynedd, poisoned at the hall for a reward, who swore the house would be plagued while his head was away.

A farmhouse beside St Teilo's holy well at Llandeilo kept the brainpan of a skull that before the Reformation was shown as the saint's own. Patients drank the well water from it until recently and many cures were recorded, though the skull probably belonged to a young woman.
